title: Be to + infinitive; be about to + infinitive

sections.title: Be to + infinitive: news, formal arrangements, controllable events
sections.content:
Be to + infinitive is commonly used in news reports to talk about events that are likely to happen in the near future:
• Police officers are to visit every home in the area.
• The main Rome-to-Naples railway line is to be reopened today. (passive form)
It is also used to talk about formal or official arrangements, formal instructions, and to give orders:
• You are not to leave the school without my permission.
• The European Parliament is to introduce a new law on safety at work.
• Children are not to be left unsupervised in the museum. (passive form)
Passive forms are often used to make orders and instructions more impersonal.
We only use be to + infinitive to talk about future events that can be controlled by people. Compare:
• In the next few years, thousands of speed cameras are to appear on major roads. (or … will appear …) and
• Scientists say they can't predict when or where the disease will appear again. (not … the disease is to appear again; the appearance of the disease can't be controlled)
• The President is to return to Brazil later today. (or … will return …) and
• The comet will return to our solar system in around 500 years. (not The comet is to return …; the movement of the comet can't be controlled)
However, when be to + infinitive refers to the future from the past (see Unit 14B), we often use it to describe what happened before something else, whether they were able to influence events or not:
• Matthew Flinders joined the Navy in 1789, but it was to be a further six years before his first voyage to Australia.
• Jeanne Pelletier was to write two more books about her experiences in Africa before her death in 1997.

sections.title: Be to + infinitive in if-clauses
sections.content:
We often use be to + infinitive in if-clauses to say that something must happen first (in the main clause) before something else can happen (in the if-clause):
• If the human race is to survive, we must look at environmental problems now.
• The law needs to be revised if justice is to be done. (passive form)
Compare the use of be to + infinitive and the present simple for the future in if-clauses:
• If López is to win gold at the next Olympics, he needs to work on his fitness. and
• If López wins gold at the next Olympics, he has said that he will retire from athletics.
Note how the order of cause and effects in if-sentences is reversed with these two tenses:
• If López is to win gold … (= effect), he needs to work … (= cause) and
• If López wins gold … (= cause), he has said that he will retire … (= effect)

sections.title: Be about to + infinitive: very near future
sections.content:
We use be about to + infinitive mainly in conversation to say that something will (not) happen in the very near future:
• We're about to eat. Do you want to join us?
• Appearing on TV might make her famous, but it's not about to make her rich.
• A: Why don't you switch it off and turn it back on again?
• B: Yes, I was about to try that when you came in. (not Yes, I was to try …) (referring to the future from the past)

exercises.question: Gil Moritz has written his first new play for 15 years. Its first performance ___ at the New Victoria Theatre.
exercises.hint: Formal announcement of a planned/controlled future event → be to + infinitive (passive).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is to be staged
Formal announcement of a planned/controlled future event → be to + infinitive (passive). Choose the passive form that matches the tense and aspect of the active version.

exercises.question: The new safety system ___ trains automatically if they pass a danger signal.
exercises.hint: Official/formal arrangement or instruction → be to + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is to stop
Official/formal arrangement or instruction → be to + infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.question: Stafford Boys' School ___ with the nearby Bicton Girls' School to form a new co-educational establishment.
exercises.hint: Official planned event reported as news → be to + infinitive (passive).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is to be merged
Official planned event reported as news → be to + infinitive (passive). Choose the passive form that matches the tense and aspect of the active version.

exercises.question: There are fears that sea levels ___ catastrophically in the next 50 years.
exercises.hint: Prediction about an uncontrollable natural event → will (not be to).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will rise
Prediction about an uncontrollable natural event → will (not be to). Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: The Prime Minister ___ (give) a press conference at noon.
exercises.hint: Formal scheduled official event → be to + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is to give
'Be to + infinitive' expresses formally scheduled or officially arranged future events. It is common in news and official contexts. It sounds more formal and certain than 'is going to'.

exercises.question: The old design and technology programme ___ with a new computer science course.
exercises.hint: Formal/official arrangement → be to + infinitive (passive).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is to be replaced
Formal/official arrangement → be to + infinitive (passive). Choose the passive form that matches the tense and aspect of the active version.

exercises.question: Managing Director Lars Lindberg, 59, ___ this summer a year early. He ___ by Christina Fontana, who joined the company last year.
options: is to retire / is to be succeeded
exercises.hint: News report about a formal official change → be to + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is to retire / is to be succeeded
News report about a formal official change → be to + infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.question: As the temperatures fall with the onset of winter, the refugee crisis ___ more severe.
exercises.hint: Predicted natural/uncontrollable event → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is to become
Predicted natural/uncontrollable event → will.

exercises.question: Seventy new posts ___ at the factory following a major investment by the parent company in the United States.
exercises.hint: Official planned event in news register → be to + infinitive (passive).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are to be created
Official planned event in news register → be to + infinitive (passive). Choose the passive form that matches the tense and aspect of the active version.

exercises.question: Watch out! The vase ___ (fall)!
exercises.hint: Immediate future, something is on the verge of happening → be about to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is about to fall
'Be about to + infinitive' expresses an action that is going to happen very soon — in the immediate future. The warning 'watch out' confirms the imminence.

exercises.question: The recent rapid rise in house prices in the south-east ___ the demand for higher salaries among lower-paid workers.
exercises.hint: Informal prediction about consequences → will (not an official/formal plan).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is to become
Informal prediction about consequences → will (not an official/formal plan).

exercises.question: You need to work much harder if you have / are to have any chance of passing the exam.
exercises.hint: If-clause condition meaning 'if you are going to have' → be to + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are to have (must have = condition)
If-clause condition meaning 'if you are going to have' → be to + infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.question: My sister is to start / is about to start a PhD in Physics.
options: is about to start (= very soon)
exercises.hint: Conversation about something happening very soon → be about to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is about to start (= very soon)
Conversation about something happening very soon → be about to.

exercises.question: Mrs Patel is likely to become Foreign Minister if the party wins / is to win power.
options: wins (= if she wins, she'll become minister)
exercises.hint: Effect depends on the winning → present simple in the if-clause.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: wins (= if she wins, she'll become minister)
Effect depends on the winning → present simple in the if-clause.

exercises.question: You ___ (not / leave) until you've finished your homework.
exercises.hint: Prohibition/instruction (authority figure) → be to + infinitive negative.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are not to leave
Negative 'be to + infinitive' expresses prohibition or a strict instruction, often from an authority figure. It is stronger and more formal than 'must not' in written or official contexts.

exercises.question: If you enjoy / are to enjoy romantic comedies, then this is a film you must see.
options: enjoy (= present simple for general truth)
exercises.hint: General condition (if you like...) → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: enjoy (= present simple for general truth)
General condition (if you like...) → present simple.

exercises.question: B: Sorry, I'm just to go / I'm just about to go home. It'll have to wait until tomorrow.
options: I'm just about to go (very imminent departure)
exercises.hint: 'Just about to' emphasises immediacy → be about to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I'm just about to go (very imminent departure)
'Just about to' emphasises immediacy → be about to.

exercises.question: If Beckman recovers / is to recover from a foot injury, it seems certain that he will play in Saturday's match.
options: recovers (= if he recovers → he'll play; cause/effect)
exercises.hint: Effect depends on recovery → present simple in if-clause.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: recovers (= if he recovers → he'll play; cause/effect)
Effect depends on recovery → present simple in if-clause.

exercises.question: Jonas Fischer has denied that he is to resign / is about to resign as marketing manager.
exercises.hint: Both 'formal announcement-style' and 'imminent' interpretations are valid here.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both are possible
Both 'formal announcement-style' and 'imminent' interpretations are valid here.

exercises.question: If the railway system is improved / is to be improved, the government should invest substantial amounts of money now.
options: is to be improved (= condition for action)
exercises.hint: Condition that must be met for the action to follow → be to + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is to be improved (= condition for action)
Condition that must be met for the action to follow → be to + infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.
